# Results

## The article is already a strong noun lever

With the intervention off, inserting `an` versus `a` moves the
full-vocabulary noun distribution by TV \(0.937\) \([0.891,0.975]\) on
the 20 held-out prompts. A transformers-only baseline, with no sparse
intervention, gives TV \(0.940\) \([0.893,0.976]\) on the same 20 prompts
and TV \(0.975\) \([0.964,0.983]\) on 95 released `an`-target occupations;
the top-1 noun changes on every prompt in both splits. Any sparse handle
that flips the article therefore has a large, generic continuation
channel available before leftover internal control is considered.

## Free generation looks coordinated; replay and rescue split it

Amplifying S1 at \(5\times\) moves every held-out prompt to `an` and
changes the greedy noun on 19/20 prompts (@tbl-packaging). Concrete twins
include `a pilot`\(\rightarrow\)`an aviator` and
`a lawyer`\(\rightarrow\)`an attorney`. Matched random features and S3 do
not produce this switch. Those free-generation rates show that S1 is a
specific handle on orthographically article-class-consistent completions. They do not identify
the transmission route.

| Condition | \(N\) | \(\Delta\) art.\ logit favors `an` | Noun token preserved | Class shift | Wrapper-like | Package-like | Twin match |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| S1 \(5\times\) | 20 | 1.00 | 0.05 | 0.95 | 0.00 | 0.95 | 0.35 |
| S1 control | 20 | 0.70 | 1.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| S3 \(5\times\) | 20 | 0.70 | 0.95 | 0.05 | 0.00 | 0.05 | 0.00 |

: Free-generation metrics (held-out occupations). Wrapper-like = generated
article moves and noun token stays; package-like = article-class-consistent
switch. These rates do not identify leftover noun control.
{#tbl-packaging}

The six-cell split does. S1 at \(5\times\) selects `an` on 20/20 prompts.
Inserting that treated article with the intervention **off** reproduces
the S1-on top-1 noun on 20/20 prompts. Across all 20 prompts, total TV is
\(0.893\), token-substitution TV is \(0.891\), and matched-prefix leftover
TV is \(0.028\) \([0.021,0.035]\) (@tbl-mediation; @fig-mediation A).
Cosine of \(E_M\) with \(E_T\) is \(0.949\) \([0.849,1.000]\); cosine of
\(E_R\) with \(E_T\) is \(0.124\) \([-0.112,0.355]\). Reconstruction
\(\|E_T-(E_M+E_R)\|_1\) is numerically zero (implementation check).
Frozen attention in the original S1 factorial yields the same qualitative
split.

| Attention | Total TV | Token-substitution TV | Leftover TV under treated article | Treated-token top-1 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Recomputed (primary) | 0.893 | 0.891 | 0.028 [0.021, 0.035] | 1.00 |
| Frozen (ablation) | 0.893 | 0.891 | 0.026 [0.020, 0.033] | 1.00 |

: S1 \(5\times\) six-cell split on all 20 held-out prompts. Intervals are
prompt-bootstrap 95\% intervals.
{#tbl-mediation}

The remaining forced cell supplies the complementary rescue. Restoring the
baseline article while leaving S1 active restores the baseline top noun on
20/20 prompts; the on/off distributional difference under that restored
article is TV \(0.030\) \([0.025,0.036]\) (@fig-mediation B). Thus the
treated article is sufficient to phenocopy the treated top noun, and the
baseline article is sufficient to rescue the baseline top noun despite the
upstream intervention. The leftover is not exactly zero: on seven listed
twins, target-minus-source \(\Delta\Delta\) is \(0.018\)
\([-0.071,0.107]\) under inserted `a` and \(0.089\) \([0.027,0.152]\)
under inserted `an`.

![S1 vector split, treated-token phenocopy and baseline-token rescue, and the prompt-aligned article-boundary jump under greedy decoding.](manuscript/figures/fig_mediation_decomposition.png){#fig-mediation width=92%}

## Prompt-aligned boundaries expose discrete causal amplification

We binary-search each prompt's S1 gain until its article margin is
bracketed by two gains separated by at most \(0.0039\), the chosen search
tolerance rather than an estimated physical width. Nineteen of 20 prompts
cross between gains 1 and 5. Under greedy decoding, the cross-boundary
noun change is TV \(0.938\) \([0.889,0.978]\); token substitution alone is
TV \(0.939\) \([0.889,0.977]\), with cosine \(0.9998\) \([0.9996,0.9999]\)
to the total (@fig-mediation C). Over the same interval, the fixed-`a`
distribution moves TV \(0.014\) \([0.009,0.019]\) and the fixed-`an`
distribution moves TV \(0.014\) \([0.010,0.017]\). The existence of an
argmax discontinuity is architectural and therefore unsurprising; the
empirical result is that this particular boundary exposes an approximately
\(0.94\)-TV continuation change while the two fixed-prefix paths remain
locally smooth. Greedy decoding therefore converts a tiny continuous
change into a nearly maximal downstream jump: a discrete causal
amplification, not a comparably large persistent latent rewrite.

The equal-looking endpoint margins in the original table require a
correction. Model, CLT, residual, and native logits are bfloat16; the
native dense grids contain only three distinct article margins. With the
same upstream states but a float32 normalization/unembedding readout, the
three audited grids contain 43 distinct margins across 51 gains and all
three cross zero. A float32 binary search narrows the bracket to
\(0.000244\); cross-boundary free TV remains \(0.992\)
\([0.989,0.997]\), whereas fixed-`a` and fixed-`an` TV are \(0.009\) and
\(0.004\), respectively. Thus \(0/0.125\) was a finite-precision artifact,
not evidence for a physical logit quantum; the high-gain argmax relay is
the robust result.

Nor is relay dominance confined to greedy decoding. Across article
temperatures \(0.1,0.25,0.5,1\), total TV declines smoothly from \(0.456\)
to \(0.057\), and the component produced by changing only the article
policy declines from \(0.454\) to \(0.055\). The matched-policy leftover
stays near \(0.015\); policy/total vector cosine ranges from \(0.999\) to
\(0.957\). At \(\tau=1\), `a`/`an` retain about 90% of article probability
mass. The public route is therefore a temperature-dependent gain channel,
not merely an argmax pathology (@fig-boundary-policy).

![Finite-precision audit and stochastic article-policy decomposition. Float32 final-head readout resolves the native bfloat16 plateaus; policy-mediated TV tracks total TV across temperature while the matched-policy leftover remains small.](manuscript/figures/fig_boundary_precision_policy.png){#fig-boundary-policy width=92%}

## Supporting controls: dose, families, and exploratory S2 localization

At \(1.5\times\), S1 writes `an` on only \(2/20\) prompts and total TV
collapses to \(0.065\). The leftover under inserted `an` is already
present: TV \(0.015\) and twin \(\Delta\Delta\) \(0.098\)
\([0.027,0.161]\). At \(3\times\), free `an` rises to \(0.90\), total TV
to \(0.802\), and token substitution still dominates. The dramatic
free-generation rewrite is therefore gated by whether the gain is large
enough to engage the article boundary of TV \(0.937\). The small leftover
under `an` is not created only by \(5\times\).

Appendix H compares \(5\times\) handles. Only S1 produces a large
free-generation article+noun switch, and that switch remains
token-substitution dominated. S3 does not move nouns. S2 never writes
`an`; greedy strings often derail, but under fixed `an` all seven twins
move toward their target (\(\Delta\Delta=+0.830\)). We classify S2 as
**exploratory evidence for a sparse fixed-token, vowel-class-aligned
effect mixed with free-generation disruption**. The S1 leftover under
`an` overlaps the random control, so we do not claim a specific noun plan
from that residual. An exploratory within-set decomposition identifies
L5/F383 as the principal carrier on the same 20 evaluation prompts
(Appendix I); it may encode vowel class, and only four matched controls
exist (\(p=0.20\)).

Appendices E--G establish cross-token reachability, stack sensitivity, and
estimand polarity: S1 changes later CLT activations; a layer-12 full-residual
reference moves target logits; and known article-only versus persistent
generators yield leftover TV \(0\) versus \(0.667\), respectively.

## Target-specific influence survives from the pre-article position

The stronger pre-article reference tests the missing
\(t\rightarrow t+2\) route. Layer 12 is selected on four development
pairs (Appendix J). On 12 disjoint same-article-class pairs, patching the
target-cued full residual at \(P\) while inserting the shared native
article `a` shifts the target-minus-source contrast by \(+1.339\) logits
\([1.021,1.677]\), compared with \(+0.215\) \([0.081,0.357]\) for ten
matched-norm random directions averaged within pair. The paired difference
is \(D=1.123\) \([0.858,1.440]\) (@fig-public-private A). The mean
full-vocabulary TV is \(0.073\) \([0.054,0.095]\). Before the patch the
mean target-minus-source gap is \(-4.302\) logits
\([-5.214,-3.422]\); the patch closes \(0.312\) \([0.265,0.371]\) of that
gap and moves mean target rank from \(12.2\) to \(4.4\), with top-10 entry
rising from \(8/12\) to \(11/12\). The target does not become top-1 on any
held-out pair, so this is target-specific private-state capacity, not
persistence-dominant behavioral control.

The same patch remains target-aligned under inserted `an`:
\(\Delta\Delta=+0.703\) \([0.526,0.875]\), versus \(+0.120\)
\([0.029,0.215]\) for matched random directions; the paired difference is
\(D=0.583\) \([0.417,0.761]\). Crossing public article with private patch
yields a public effect of \(+0.609\) logits \([0.224,0.984]\) with the
private patch off and \(-0.026\) \([-0.385,0.359]\) with it on
(@fig-public-private B). The interaction is
\(\Gamma=-0.635\) \([-0.839,-0.448]\). Matched random patches have a small
positive interaction \(+0.095\) \([0.019,0.171]\); the paired
target-minus-random interaction is \(-0.731\) \([-0.971,-0.498]\)
(@fig-public-private C). Article-prefix compatibility therefore modulates
the private target-state effect. Inserted `an` is mismatched for both
consonant-initial alternatives, so the negative interaction may reflect
grammatical mismatch, saturation, or support shifts toward other
vowel-initial nouns; we do not interpret it as an allocation trade-off
between two registers. Public token identity and private upstream state
are separately intervenable and non-additive in this target-constructed
reference. This does not show that a sparse feature allocates the same
lexical state between those routes.

![A pre-article target residual moves held-out nouns under a fixed visible article more than matched random directions; the raw \(2\times 2\) surface and the random-controlled interaction show that article-prefix compatibility modulates the private effect. Error bars are pair-bootstrap 95\% intervals.](manuscript/figures/fig_pre_article_public_private.png){#fig-public-private width=90%}

## Natural-state-derived residuals isolate private influence but not a carrier switch

Natural occupation descriptions reproduce target-specific private
influence without naming the target noun. The pooled development sweep
selects layer 12. Under a fixed article, target patches move the
target-minus-source logit by \(0.776\) \([0.484,1.115]\) on 12
cross-class pairs and \(0.964\) \([0.667,1.266]\) on 12 same-class pairs.
Wrong-target patches yield only \(0.146\) and \(0.130\), respectively;
sign-reversed patches move the contrast in the opposite direction. The
effect decomposes into target-logit enhancement (\(+0.526\) cross-class;
\(+0.839\) same-class) plus smaller source suppression
(\(-0.250\) and \(-0.125\)). Target probability rises in both regimes,
while total occupation-vocabulary mass does not reliably increase.

Crucially, the natural patch changes the greedy article on 0/12 pairs in either
regime. Under greedy decoding, token-substitution TV is therefore zero and the
observed free-path TV---\(0.049\) cross-class and \(0.059\) same-class---survives
token fixing. The stochastic audit qualifies this statement: at
\(\tau=0.1\), public TV is 0.002 cross-class and 0.000 same-class, but at
\(\tau=1\) it rises to 0.063 and 0.059 while private TV remains 0.049 and
0.064. The patch is private-dominant under low-temperature article policies,
not exclusively private under every policy. This strengthens the evidence for
a natural private route, but it
does **not** reveal prompting regimes that reallocate causal state between
public and private carriers. Same versus cross article class changes
effect size, not channel identity (@fig-natural-regimes).

![Natural target-residual patches produce target-specific fixed-token effects in both article-class regimes and outperform wrong-target and matched-norm controls; no greedy article switch occurs.](manuscript/figures/fig_natural_carrier_regimes.png){#fig-natural-regimes width=91%}

## Semantically valid synonyms recruit different routes under lexical constraints

The matched synonym task removes the semantic-truth component of the earlier
correctness confound: both lexical realizations answer the same occupational
definition. It does not remove instruction-related resistance. The evaluated
source prompt explicitly requests the source noun's first letter, whereas the
target-state donor prompt requests the target noun's first letter; cross-initial
target movement therefore conflicts with the visible evaluated instruction.
Eligibility and family
deduplication leave six between-article and eight within-`a` semantic families
at 1B. Leave-one-family-out selection independently chooses layer 18 in every
fold. At native strength, the held-out fixed-target-article lexical effect is
\(0.250\ [0.167,0.375]\) logits between article classes and
\(0.227\ [0.133,0.328]\) within class. Wrong-target effects are only 0.073
and 0.055; sign-reversed directions are \(-0.021\) and \(-0.125\).
Thus both regimes clear local efficacy before route comparison.

The route phenotype then separates sharply. All 6/6 between-class patches
switch the greedy article, whereas 0/8 within-class patches do. At
\(\tau=1\), between-class public TV is
\(0.423\ [0.352,0.483]\), compared with private TV
\(0.030\ [0.019,0.045]\). Within class, public TV is only
\(0.030\ [0.018,0.047]\), while private TV is
\(0.038\ [0.025,0.053]\). Distributional magnitude alone is insufficient, so
we also project each vector onto the intended target-minus-source noun
direction. The between-class public component is strongly target aligned
(0.370 probability contrast, \([0.212,0.523]\)); its private component is
0.018. Within class the public component is approximately zero and slightly
negative (\(-0.003\)), while the private component is positive
(0.029 \([0.008,0.054]\)).

Define each family's route contrast as public TV minus private TV. The
difference between the between- and within-article route contrasts is
\(0.401\ [0.335,0.453]\) at native strength and \(\tau=1\); exact
family-label permutation gives \(p=0.00033\). The target-aligned interaction is
\(0.384\ [0.229,0.529]\). Both interactions remain positive at every tested
strength and temperature (@fig-correctness-carriers D). The same-target-letter
control is appreciable between class (0.172 logits on four available families),
consistent with the patch carrying coarse orthographic/article information,
but remains below the target patch; within class it is 0.031 on two available
families.

The simple effects support the stronger term *double dissociation* only for the
scientifically primary signed lexical projection. Between classes,
public-minus-private target influence is (0.352\ [0.200,0.498]\), exact
one-sided sign-flip (p=0.0156\). Within class, private-minus-public target
influence is (0.032\ [0.010,0.059]\), (p=0.00391\). For unsigned TV, the
between-class public-minus-private effect is (0.393\ [0.325,0.445]\),
(p=0.0156\), but the within-class private-minus-public effect is only
(0.008\ [-0.003,0.020]\), (p=0.117\). Thus the full-distribution result is a
route interaction, while the target-aligned result independently establishes
both simple effects. The evidence supports mediator-relative distinguishability:
when article identity distinguishes two correct lexical alternatives, the
intervention recruits a strong public relay; within one article-equivalence
class, target-aligned influence remains private. It does not imply that all
private state is transferred into the public token.

We attempted the stricter paired test using the same source noun and semantic
definition with both a same-article and cross-article target. Three frozen,
outcome-blind construction banks contained 23, 22, and 70 candidate triples.
Only the events/organization meaning passed all single-token, article-policy,
and four lexical-preference rules (the exhaustive bank produced two source
orderings of that one family). The dominant failures were article-policy
mismatch and failure of the within-target prompt to favor its intended synonym.
Because this falls below the predeclared 8--15-family target, we do not run or
interpret a causal triad assay. This is a behavioral construction failure of the
current first-letter task, not evidence against the route hypothesis.

![Correctness-preserving synonym double dissociation in Gemma 3 1B PT. The same cross-validated residual-patch procedure is locally effective in both regimes (A), but between-article distinctions are public-relay dominant whereas within-article distinctions retain target-aligned private influence (B--C). The route interaction is positive across every patch strength and article-policy temperature (D). Error bars and bands are semantic-family bootstrap 95\% intervals.](manuscript/figures/fig_correctness_preserving_carriers.png){#fig-correctness-carriers width=97%}

## A closed-loop gain law predicts public influence

Across 32 features selected on disjoint occupations, article attribution
predicts induced article-margin change at 270M (Spearman \(\rho=0.530\),
bootstrap 95\% CI \([0.200,0.772]\)) and transfers directionally at 1B
(\(0.432\ [0.014,0.729]\)). This is evidence for local calibration, not by
itself a channel label. The earlier TV comparisons also mixed signed,
target-specific attributions with unsigned distributional distances. In the
matched reanalysis, signed future attribution versus signed fixed-token
target-minus-source change is \(0.270\ [-0.100,0.584]\) at 270M and
\(-0.129\ [-0.451,0.225]\) at 1B; signed target-logit correlations are
\(0.307\ [-0.047,0.594]\) and \(0.120\ [-0.279,0.473]\). Absolute attribution
versus absolute target effect is also undetectable. These panels therefore do
not reliably rank persistent target effects under this protocol, but their wide
intervals do not establish independence or a general attribution failure.

The public route admits a positive predictive account. Under a conditional
two-article policy, let \(q_i=P(B=an\mid I=i)\) and let \(Y_a,Y_{an}\) be the
intervention-off noun distributions under fixed articles. Then

$$
E_{\mathrm{public}}=(q_1-q_0)(Y_{an}-Y_a),\qquad
TV(E_{\mathrm{public}})=|q_1-q_0|TV(Y_{an},Y_a).
$$

Thus downstream public influence factorizes into **policy movement** and
**continuation leverage**. Policy movement is in turn determined by the
baseline article margin, intervention-induced margin change, and temperature.
This factorization is an elementary consequence of the two-branch mixture, not
the empirical novelty. The scientific test is whether its factors can be
measured separately and predict unseen interventions better than attribution or
decoder context alone. The identity holds numerically to \(1.3\times10^{-7}\).

At 270M and \(\tau=0.1\), two-way holdout excludes both the test feature and
test prompt while retaining intervention-off prompt quantities. Constant,
attribution-only, susceptibility-only, branch-leverage-only, and activation
baselines have \(R^2=-0.052,-0.547,-0.082,-0.052,-0.045\), respectively.
Calibrating attribution to local margin movement and composing it with decoder
susceptibility yields \(0.827\); adding prompt-specific branch leverage yields
\(0.840\), with calibration slope 0.960. The full model remains
\(R^2=0.840\)--\(0.875\) across \(\tau=0.1\) to 1 under combined feature--prompt
holdout. Thus the large gain is not explained by boundary proximity alone.
Because `a/an` branch leverage is uniformly high, its incremental contribution
is modest; this task stresses susceptibility more strongly than leverage.

At 1B, susceptibility alone is the strongest simple baseline at low temperature
(two-way \(R^2=0.270\)), while the full composition reaches only 0.194 and
becomes non-positive at higher temperatures. Holding out prompts alone is less
severe (full \(R^2=0.400\) at \(\tau=0.1\)); holding out feature identity exposes
the weak transferable local calibration. Using measured margin movement and
actual branch leverage is an accounting oracle with \(R^2=1\), not a predictive
result. Local causal pressure, boundary susceptibility, and branch leverage are
therefore distinct measurable factors, but only the 270M panel currently
supports strong out-of-sample prediction (@fig-attribution-calibration).

![Local and matched-estimand calibration plus public-effect prediction. C compares attribution-only and full-composition predictions with observed public TV for unseen 270M feature--prompt cells at \(\tau=0.1\); D shows that the 270M result survives simple baselines, whereas 1B transfer remains weak.](manuscript/figures/fig_attribution_channel_calibration.png){#fig-attribution-calibration width=92%}

## At 1B, the ladder separates weak, support-invalid, and hybrid sparse handles

The frozen 1B top-four/\(5\times\) S1 recipe fails the first stage: on held-out
prompts it moves the `an`-minus-`a` margin by only 0.075 logits on average and
crosses toward `an` on 1/20 prompts. The original selection label is also
miscalibrated to the contrast: it requires positive attribution to `an`, not to
`an` minus `a`, and several features raise both article logits.

Re-ranking the frozen 270M development graphs by the corrected positive
`an-a`-margin plus future-target criterion retains two canonical S1 members
(L12/F6229 and L13/F10231) and replaces the two weakest-margin members. Thus
the canonical 270M intervention is not a perfectly harmonized scale comparator,
although its two dominant corrected-margin features and its held-out relay
phenotype remain intact. We treat cross-scale sparse comparisons as diagnostic,
not as a controlled scale effect.

Development-only margin calibration repairs the binary contrast. The frozen
top-24/\(20\times\) coalition moves the development margin by 3.461 logits and
the held-out margin by 3.488, closely matching 270M S1. But it fails mediator
specificity: `a` or `an` remains the top token on only 3/20 held-out prompts;
17/20 instead begin with alternatives such as `called`. Fixed branches show
matched-prefix TV 0.097 \([0.069,0.127]\) under inserted `a` and 0.266
\([0.147,0.394]\) under inserted `an`, but the intended public-token split is
identified on only two prompts whose off/on free mediators are both articles.
We therefore do not assign this sparse intervention a 1B transmission
phenotype.

A development-only constrained frontier search provides a less destructive
operating point. We maximize corrected `an-a` margin movement subject to
100\% article-mediator-support validity, mean full-vocabulary KL at most 0.1, article
mass at least 0.5, and small feature count. The frozen optimum is the single
feature L18/F5015 at \(7.5\times\): development margin movement is 0.859,
article mass 0.935, and mean KL 0.077. On 20 held-out prompts it preserves an
`a/an` top token on 20/20 and changes the greedy article on only 1/20. Greedy
switch counts are not the final assay: under conditional stochastic policies,
the held-out margin movement is 0.500 \([0.344,0.675]\) logits. At \(\tau=0.1\),
mean article-policy movement is 0.039, public TV is 0.026
\([0.00002,0.078]\), and matched-policy private TV is 0.012
\([0.007,0.019]\). At \(\tau=1\), policy movement is 0.067, public TV is 0.055
\([0.037,0.074]\), and private TV remains 0.013 \([0.008,0.019]\); public/total
vector cosine is 0.767. The gain identity predicts public TV to numerical
precision. Thus the mediator-valid sparse 1B handle has a low-amplitude hybrid
effect that becomes public-relay dominant under softer article policies, despite
only one greedy switch.

| Model/intervention | Local efficacy | Mediator-support validity | Identified channel |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 270M S1, top-4/\(5\times\) | 3.313-logit mean margin movement | `a/an` 20/20 | Public-relay dominant |
| 1B original S1, top-4/\(5\times\) | 0.075 | `a/an` 20/20 | Not identified: weak handle |
| 1B margin S1, top-24/\(20\times\) | 3.488 | `a/an` 3/20 | Not identified: mediator-invalid |
| 1B frontier L18/F5015, \(7.5\times\) | 0.500 held out | `a/an` 20/20 | Hybrid; public-dominant by \(\tau=1\) |
| 1B natural-state-derived residual, native strength | target \(\Delta\Delta=0.846/1.312\) | fixed visible article | Private target influence |
| 1B correctness-preserving synonyms, native strength | target \(\Delta\Delta=0.250/0.227\) | `a/an` support; both synonyms valid | Public/private double dissociation |

: Local efficacy and channel identification are sequential requirements.
Cross-/same-class natural-residual values are separated by a slash.
{#tbl-cross-scale-stage}

The natural-state-derived residual comparison supplies the valid 1B private assay. A pooled
development sweep selects layer 14/25 (relative depth 0.56). At natural
strength, held-out target \(\Delta\Delta\) is 0.846 cross-class and 1.312
same-class, compared with 0.776 and 0.964 at 270M; target top-1 rises only to
0/12 and 1/12. Private TV is 0.054 and 0.039, versus 0.049 and 0.059 at 270M,
so scale does not uniformly increase distributional private influence. At
\(\tau=0.1\), the 1B public component is 0.002 cross-class and zero same-class
while private TV is 0.055 and 0.039; at \(\tau=1\), public TV rises to 0.074
and 0.027 while private TV remains 0.062 and 0.046. The defensible scale result
is target-directed movement at both scales without behavioral sufficiency or a
monotone scale effect. Normalizing by the baseline gap, the 1B patch closes
0.083 of the cross-class gap and 0.272 within class, versus 0.103 and 0.249 at
270M. Patch-norm-normalized effects favor 1B, but distributional private TV and
rank improvement do not; the conclusion depends on the estimand.

The apparent strength-by-class public recruitment is also not robust. The
difference-in-differences from strength 0.5 to 1.5 is 0.063 at \(\tau=0.1\)
and 0.055 at \(\tau=1\), but pair-bootstrap intervals include zero at every
temperature. The low-temperature contrast is driven by the sole cross-class
pair whose greedy article switches at strength 1.5; private influence remains
simultaneously present. We classify this as a suggestive candidate regime, not
a demonstrated carrier switch.

The independent 1B feature calibration supplies a directional cross-scale
generalization. Article attribution again predicts held-out local margin
movement across 32 individually amplified features (\(\rho=0.432\), bootstrap
95\% CI \([0.014,0.729]\)); leave-one-feature-out estimates remain positive
\([0.375,0.478]\), largest-effect exclusion gives \(0.375\), and the partial
rank correlation controlling layer, held-out activation, and decoder norm is
\(0.352\). We do not use the previously reported above-median-efficacy subset
as confirmatory evidence because it conditions on a realized outcome. The
matched signed target analyses above retain all features and avoid an
all-held-out-prompt mediator gate.

| Scale | Article attr. \(\to\) local margin | Future attr. \(\to\) fixed target logit | Future attr. \(\to\) target-source |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 270M (32 features) | \(0.530\ [0.200,0.772]\) | \(0.307\ [-0.047,0.594]\) | \(0.270\ [-0.100,0.584]\) |
| 1B (32 features) | \(0.432\ [0.014,0.729]\) | \(0.120\ [-0.279,0.473]\) | \(-0.129\ [-0.451,0.225]\) |

: Across-scale matched-estimand feature calibration. Values are feature-level
Spearman correlations with feature-bootstrap 95\% intervals.

## The released `is/are` task fails at local efficacy in these PT models

The second-mediator experiment does not support route recruitment. Development
selection is itself nearly flat: the best pooled layer has mean target
\(\Delta\Delta=0\) at 270M and 0.063 at 1B. At frozen natural strength on eight
held-out animals, the fixed-native-verb target contrast for \(1\to3\) is
\(-0.031\ [-0.078,0.031]\) at 270M and
\(-0.031\ [-0.094,0.031]\) at 1B. For \(3\to5\), it is exactly 0 at both
scales, with intervals \([-0.047,0.047]\). Wrong-target controls are comparable,
and no greedy verb switches occur at any tested strength.

Distributional movement survives fixed verbs but is not target aligned. At
\(\tau=1\), native-strength private TV ranges from 0.015 to 0.020 across
scale/regime cells, whereas public TV ranges only from 0.0006 to 0.0032.
Because the intervention does not move the intended number contrast, those TVs
measure generic state perturbation rather than private arithmetic control. This
negative result is a direct use of the ladder: the experiment stops at local
efficacy and cannot adjudicate whether `is/are` capacity controls externalization
in these pretrained models (@fig-is-are).

![Second-mediator stress test on the pinned `is/are` subtraction dataset. Target-derived residual patches do not move the intended number contrast at either scale; small fixed-verb distributional changes are therefore not interpreted as target-specific private transmission.](manuscript/figures/fig_is_are_carrier_capacity.png){#fig-is-are width=90%}

## Measurement audits bound the 1B interpretation

The 1B affine CLT reproduces task logits closely but not every internal state.
Across four selection prompts and five representative layers, mean MLP-output
reconstruction cosine is 0.803 and normalized MSE is 0.341. The affine skip
norm averages 0.714 of the native output norm (sparse and skip terms are not
orthogonal), while reconstructed article-margin and future-target logits differ
from native values by only 0.031 and 0.063 logits on average. Layerwise cosine
ranges from 0.600 at layer 14 to 0.998 at layer 0. Weak sparse control therefore
cannot be cleanly attributed to model scale rather than dictionary geometry.

Graph coverage is less concerning. On a representative prompt, raising the cap
from 1,200 to 2,400 includes all 2,085 article-graph and 2,205 future-graph
active features. The original cap retains 100\% of pre-article absolute margin
attribution, 99.7\% of future attribution, and 95\% overlap with the full-graph
top 20. Because 2,400 already saturates both graphs, a 4,800 cap is redundant.
Direct pre-article ranking over the saturated graph retains the same leading
corrected-margin candidates, including the frontier feature. These audits make
simple graph truncation unlikely for this case, while leaving CLT
reconstruction and intervention construction as live explanations.
